paras: The threatened lynching of Ben Riley took place in Grafton, West Virginia, in March 1903, when Riley, a Black day cook at the Painter boarding house, was accused of assaulting a chambermaid there. He was arrested, jailed and held for the grand jury, and the Wheeling Sunday Register reported that public anger was such that "a lynching was scarcely avoided." No violence against Riley was reported, and the threat appears in only one of the two papers that covered the case.

Benjamin Riley worked as the "colored day cook" at the Painter boarding house and restaurant on Main street in Grafton. The complainant, named as Rubana Decker in the Clarksburg Telegram and as Ruhana Becker or Miss Decker in the Register, was a chambermaid employed in the same house; the Register said she had come to Grafton a year earlier and had "borne a good reputation."

According to the Register's Grafton correspondent, Riley seized the woman while she was making up a bed upstairs, choked her, assaulted her and threatened to cut her throat with a razor if she told anyone. The Telegram described the charge only as criminal assault, under a subheading calling it an "Attempt at Criminal Assault." A warrant was issued, sworn out by the chambermaid in the Telegram's account and secured by Mr. Painter in the Register's, and Riley was arrested in the opera house and jailed overnight.

The two papers place the arrest a day apart: the Telegram said it took place on Thursday night, March 19, while the Register's March 21 dispatch dated the alleged crime to "nine o'clock last night." The next morning Riley appeared before Squire Wells, a justice, who held him to await the action of the grand jury. The Telegram said Riley waived examination, whereas the Register said Wells heard testimony from Miss Decker and the day clerk.

The accusation was not widely known in the town until after the hearing, the Telegram reported, and a crowd gathered at the justice's office to hear the details, before which Riley "was apparently very uneasy and was glad when he got back into jail." The Register went further, saying the news "startled the citizens into such a rage that a lynching was scarcely avoided" and that when the woman's "comrades" learned the facts "a lynching was scarcely averted." Neither paper described a mob forming at the jail, a threat by any named person, or any action taken by officers to protect Riley.
Riley was remanded to jail to await the grand jury. No report of an indictment, trial or outcome appears in the coverage.

The case was covered only by white newspapers in West Virginia. The Clarksburg Daily Telegram ran a brief Grafton dispatch on its front page on March 21 under the headline "NEGRO COOK IN TROUBLE," and the Clarksburg Telegram reprinted it word for word on March 27. That account was brief, reporting a charge, a hearing and a crowd, and saying nothing of lynching.

The Wheeling Sunday Register printed the story on March 22 at the head of a column of Grafton news, followed by items on a new coal mine and a drugstore opening. Its correspondent presented the accusation as fact, calling it a "revolting crime" and Riley "the brute" who carried out his "fiendish purpose," and twice mentioned the near-lynching without criticism. No Black-press coverage of the case was found.

The accounts differ on the date of the arrest, on whether Riley waived examination or testimony was heard, and on whether the alleged assault was attempted or completed. The threat of lynching itself rests on the Register's correspondent alone, while the Telegram's same-day dispatch mentions only a crowd at the hearing.

bases: Riley was arrested on an assault charge and held for the grand jury; the only sign of collective violence is the Wheeling Sunday Register's statement that a lynching was 'scarcely avoided', with a crowd gathering at the justice's office (A1, A2).

Riley was not killed or attacked: both reports say he was jailed and held for the grand jury (A1, A2); the only lynching reference is a threatened one in A2, set off by an accusation of assault on a woman.

The arrest and charge are reported independently by two papers (A1, A2), but the lynching threat that makes this an episode of racial violence rests on the Wheeling Sunday Register alone (A2); the Telegram describes only a crowd at the hearing (A1).

accounts.label: Clarksburg Telegram dispatch
accounts.gist: Riley was arrested Thursday night on a criminal assault warrant, waived examination and was remanded to jail; the crime became known only after the hearing, and Riley seemed uneasy before the crowd at the justice's office.

accounts.label: Wheeling Register correspondent
accounts.gist: A detailed account of the alleged assault, in which Riley was said to have choked the woman and threatened her with a razor; testimony was heard before Squire Wells; citizens were so enraged that a lynching was 'scarcely avoided'.

framing.detail: The Clarksburg Telegram ran a short item headed 'NEGRO COOK IN TROUBLE', calling the charge an 'Attempt at Criminal Assault' and noting Riley's unease before the crowd.

The Wheeling Sunday Register treated the accusation as fact ('revolting crime', 'the brute', 'fiendish purpose') and reported the near-lynching without condemning it, though it records that the case went through the courts.
